protocol: Per frame the rail anchors are probed at fixed ranges that lie inside the anchored span, so no extrapolation is involved. Two self-consistency facts carry the test: within a frame, an anchor-to-anchor step riding the rail_max_heading bound means the tracker was dragged rather than supported; between consecutive frames 0.1 s apart the centre at a fixed range ahead cannot move by metres. Gauge, support and rail-head height at the same anchors say whether the matched pair still looks like rails. No annotations are used.
conclusion: Track-centre lock failures are the dominant source of in-envelope cluster load: frames whose estimated centre sits more than 1 m off the sensor axis at 30 m are 14 percent of frames and carry 56 percent of all in-envelope clusters. During excursions the matched gauge is 1.575-1.62 m against 1.53-1.56 m on track, and anchor support is lower, so the estimator matched a wider pair on weaker evidence rather than following a real track. Steps riding the per-step bound occur in under 1.1 percent of steps, so this is a discrete mismatch, not a gradual walk-off. Two recordings show no excursion at all, including the one containing a switch and a platform. This is a measured association with a direct mechanism, not a proven cause: a cluttered section could both confuse the matcher and put more structure near the envelope.
